## Scope

Closes the **device identity gap**: user identity alone says nothing about
what hardware just plugged into the wall jack. The book builds port- and
SSID-level admission control — 802.1X with EAP-TLS against an NPS RADIUS
tier, Intune SCEP-issued device certificates, a five-tier VLAN policy
structure, MAB confined to documented guest/IoT exceptions, and Intune
compliance as the posture signal enforced in real time via RADIUS Change
of Authorization. Thesis: **the physical port is an identity-plane
enforcement point, and the same certificate substrate that authenticates
users must authenticate devices before they get a VLAN at all.**

## Learning objectives

- Explain why user authentication alone leaves the physical-access gap,
  and how the voice-VLAN precedent already normalized per-device network
  decisions.
- Describe the authentication stack (supplicant → authenticator → RADIUS)
  and justify EAP-TLS over credential-based EAP methods for federal use.
- Design the NPS RADIUS tier and the 802.1X port configuration (IOS-XE
  reference) including re-authentication and session timeout behavior.
- Stand up Intune SCEP device-certificate enrollment against the issuing
  CA, and state the revocation story for machine certs.
- Apply the five-tier NAC policy structure — production, remediation,
  quarantine VLANs, plus MAB-profiled guest/IoT — and defend MAB as a
  logged exception, never a default.
- Wire Intune compliance state into access decisions and trigger CoA to
  re-evaluate a live session when posture changes.
- Extend the same model to wireless via WPA3-Enterprise, and to DHCP
  fingerprinting / IPAM-driven VLAN assignment through the Book 01
  Infoblox layer.

## Key concepts

- Device identity vs. user identity; the federal physical-access reality.
- EAP-TLS mutual certificate authentication; why password-carrying EAP
  methods fail the phishing-resistance bar.
- The certificate trust chain for devices (Book 03's hierarchy applied at
  the port) and SCEP enrollment through Intune.
- Five-tier VLAN model: production / remediation / quarantine / voice /
  MAB-profiled exceptions.
- RADIUS CoA as the real-time enforcement channel for posture changes.
- RADIUS accounting into Sentinel; NAC analytics rules as slot-relevant
  telemetry.
- The NAC → ZTNA continuum: the port decision and the Conditional Access
  decision are the same decision at different layers.

## Implementation sequence (phased, per the book)

1. **Phase 1 — monitor mode (weeks 1–4):** 802.1X open/monitor on pilot
   switches; collect would-have-failed data; fix supplicants and cert
   coverage before anything blocks.
2. **Phase 2 — wired enforcement (weeks 5–10):** promote pilot closets to
   enforce; remediation/quarantine VLANs live; MAB exceptions documented.
3. **Phase 3 — wireless enforcement (weeks 11–14):** WPA3-Enterprise
   SSID cutover; retire PSK networks.
4. **Phase 4 — IoT segmentation and hardening (weeks 15–20):** DHCP
   fingerprinting, IPAM-driven VLAN assignment, CoA-driven posture
   enforcement across the estate.

## Compliance hooks

IA-3 (+1) device identification and authentication; AC-3, AC-17, AC-19,
AC-20 access enforcement surfaces; SC-7(3)(5) boundary/deny-by-default;
CM-6, CM-7, CM-8 configuration and inventory; AU-11 accounting retention.
FedRAMP 20x: KSI-CMT and KSI-IAM themes — the slot binding lands with the
adapter mapping refresh.

## Prerequisites

Book 01 (the DDI/IPAM layer NAC assigns into); Book 03 is read next but
its certificate hierarchy is the trust anchor this book consumes — skim
its trust-chain section first if certificates are new to you. Basic
switching/CLI familiarity.

## Labs

1. Configure one switch port pair in monitor mode against a lab NPS;
   review the would-have-failed log and produce the pre-enforcement
   readiness report.
2. Issue a device certificate via an Intune SCEP profile, complete an
   EAP-TLS authentication, then revoke and watch the re-auth fail into
   the quarantine VLAN.
3. Flip a device out of Intune compliance and verify CoA moves the live
   session to remediation without waiting for re-authentication.

## Pitfalls the book calls out

- Skipping monitor mode and enforcing on day one — the classic
  NAC-lockout failure; monitor-mode-first is non-negotiable.
- Letting MAB become the default path instead of a documented,
  inventoried exception — it silently converts NAC back to MAC filtering.
- Certificate expiry as an availability event: device certs that expire
  without renewal automation take the fleet off the network.
- Treating the voice VLAN as a security boundary rather than the
  precedent it is.
